front: Sound is what kind of wave?
back: Mechanical, longitudinal wave. Particles vibrate along the direction of propagation. Cannot travel through a vacuum.

front: Ultrasound is defined as any sound wave with a frequency greater than {{c1::20,000 Hz (20 kHz)}}.
Which parameter of a sound wave is determined by BOTH the source and the medium?
back: Wavelength (λ). Period and frequency are set by the source; propagation speed is set by the medium; wavelength depends on both.

front: Average speed of sound in soft tissue is {{c1::1540 m/s}} (= 1.54 mm/μs).
What two properties of the medium determine propagation speed?
back: Density and stiffness. Speed increases with stiffness and decreases with density.

front: Rank propagation speed: bone, air, fat, soft tissue, lung.
In soft tissue, wavelength (mm) = {{c1::1.54 / frequency (MHz)}}.
Does propagation speed depend on the sound wave's frequency?
back: No. All frequencies travel at the same speed through a given medium. Speed depends only on the medium.

front: High-frequency transducers give what trade-off in image quality?
back: Better axial resolution but less depth of penetration. Low-frequency transducers give the opposite.

front: Intensity is proportional to {{c1::amplitude²}}, so doubling the amplitude quadruples the intensity.
How many dB corresponds to a doubling (or halving) of signal amplitude?
How many dB corresponds to a 100× difference in amplitude?
Acoustic impedance Z = {{c1::tissue density × propagation velocity (ρ × c)}}.
What determines the amount of ultrasound reflected at a tissue interface?
back: The difference in acoustic impedance between the two tissues, and the angle of incidence (best reflection when beam is perpendicular).

front: What causes ultrasound 'dropout'?
back: The beam is parallel (not perpendicular) to the tissue interface, so little or no signal reflects back to the transducer.

front: What phenomenon produces speckle in the image?
back: Scattering — radiation of ultrasound in multiple directions from structures smaller than the wavelength (e.g., red blood cells).

front: What is the major source of ultrasound information used to build a 2-D image?
back: Backscatter (a diffuse form of reflection). Because it redirects sound in many directions, some energy always returns to the transducer.

front: What is refraction and what artifact does it cause?
back: Deflection of the ultrasound beam at an interface between tissues of different acoustic impedance. Causes double-image (edge-duplication) artifacts.

front: What is the most common mechanism of ultrasound attenuation in tissue?
back: Absorption. Attenuation also depends on transducer frequency, the tissue's attenuation coefficient, and distance from the transducer.

front: What is Time Gain Compensation (TGC)?
back: An adjustment that amplifies returning signals more with increasing depth, compensating for attenuation. Default preset: less gain near-field, more gain far-field.

front: A typical clinical ultrasound pulse contains {{c1::2–4}} cycles.
Can imaging be performed with continuous-wave (CW) ultrasound?
back: No. Anatomic imaging requires pulsed ultrasound (the system must alternate transmit and listen). CW is used for Doppler.

front: Pulse duration (μs) = {{c1::number of cycles × period}}. Typical clinical value 0.5–3 μs.
Spatial pulse length (mm) = {{c1::number of cycles × wavelength}}. Determines axial resolution.
What determines the pulse repetition period (PRP) and PRF?
back: Imaging depth. Deeper imaging → longer PRP and lower PRF. The sonographer changes only the listening time, not the pulse duration.

front: Are PRP and PRF related to transducer frequency?
back: No. PRP/PRF are set by imaging depth, not by transducer frequency. They are reciprocals of each other.

front: Round-trip time for a pulse in soft tissue = {{c1::13 μs per cm}} of depth.
For imaging depth d (cm) in soft tissue: PRP (μs) = {{c1::13 × d}} and maximum PRF (Hz) = {{c2::77,000 / d}}.
What is duty factor?
back: The fraction (or %) of time the transducer is transmitting sound. Unitless. Typically < 1% in imaging. CW = 100%; a system that is off = 0%.

front: What does a larger transducer aperture do to the beam?
back: Produces a more focused (narrower) beam. A smaller aperture allows better angulation.

front: Which parameter of a pulse is most improved by using a shorter pulse (short SPL)?
back: Axial resolution. Shorter SPL → better ability to resolve two closely spaced structures along the beam axis.

front: What two categories of bioeffects can ultrasound cause?
back: Thermal (heating from absorption) and non-thermal / mechanical (cavitation — bubble formation and collapse).

front: What safety principle governs ultrasound exposure?
back: ALARA — As Low As Reasonably Achievable. Use the lowest power and shortest exposure needed for diagnosis.

front: Increasing the transmitted power increases the {{c1::amplitude}} of reflected US signals and can produce bioeffects at excess levels.
